Now a note on scope.

Cross-session topics such as formal governance frameworks, ITSM standards, SLA and OLA, detailed disaster recovery, change models and blockchain are intentionally reserved for their corresponding sessions.
The foundational principles above support them, without expanding this guide into the entire course.
Next, the essential distinctions to retain.
Again, I will go through the table row by row, giving each pair of terms and the difference between them.
First, principle versus function.
A principle is a decision criterion, while a function is a management activity.
Second, alignment versus value.
Alignment means supporting objectives, whereas value means demonstrating benefits.
Third, measurement versus controlling.
Measurement observes results, while controlling corrects deviations.
Fourth, organising versus staffing.
Organising defines ownership, while staffing provides capable people.
Fifth, automation versus integration.
Automation executes tasks automatically, whereas integration connects systems and data.
Sixth, ERP versus CRM versus BI.
ERP concerns internal operations, CRM concerns customer relationships, and BI concerns analytics.
Seventh, cloud versus ecosystem.
Cloud is on-demand computing, whereas an ecosystem is made up of interdependent participants creating value.
Eighth, API versus interoperability.
An API is an interface, while interoperability is the ability to exchange and correctly use information.
Ninth, Agile versus Scrum.
Agile is a delivery philosophy, while Scrum is a specific framework.
Tenth, project versus operations.
A project is a temporary delivery effort, while operations means ongoing service management.
Keep these ten distinctions clear in your mind, because exam questions often test whether you can tell these neighbouring ideas apart.
